diagnostic_evidence.quote:
For $k\ge 1$, a problem $\{\Xi,\Omega,\mathcal{M},\Lambda\}$ is said to be in 
$\Sigma_k^\alpha$ if it is in $\Delta_{k+1}^\alpha$ and there exists a tower of
algorithms $\{\Gamma_{n_k,\ldots,n_1}\}$ such that 
$\Gamma_{n_k}(A) \uparrow \Xi(A)$ for all $A \in \Omega$.

issues.failure_explanation: Subtracting the error tolerance ensures only that each output lies below the corresponding exact value and converges to the desired limit. It does not make the outputs nondecreasing, so it does not establish the asserted Sigma classification. The analogous raw outputs in the examples likewise need not be monotone because the S1 covers are not assumed nested.

failure_location.quote: Let $\widetilde{\Gamma}_n(A)$ be an approximation of $f(\Gamma_n^{\spec}(A))$, computed to accuracy $1/n$ using $\Lambda$. We then set $\Gamma_n(A)=\widetilde{\Gamma}_n(A)-1/n$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace lower approximants by successive maxima and upper approximants by successive minima, while retaining suitable one-sided error corrections; then verify convergence and finite-data access.
issues.overall_effect: The one-sided SCI classifications derived by this construction are not proved with towers satisfying the paper's own monotonicity definition.
issues.title: Approximations do not provide the required monotone SCI tower
issues.why_classification: Successive extrema give a short local repair without changing any claimed SCI level or spectral guarantee.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Let $a_{k,j}$ be an approximation of ${\log(N_{\delta_k}(\Gamma_{n(\delta_k)}^{\spec}(A)))}/{\log(1/\delta_k)}$ computed to an accuracy $1/j$.

issues.failure_explanation: The inner limit is the supremum of the ratios formed from the cover counts, not from $N_{\delta_k}(\spec(A))$. The factor-three estimate only shows that the cover and spectrum ratios have the same eventual limsup; it does not justify the displayed equality for fixed $n_2$.

failure_location.quote:
If we define $
\Gamma_{n_2,n_1}(A)=\max_{n_2\leq k\leq n_1}a_{k,n_1}$, then
$$
\lim_{n_1\rightarrow\infty}\Gamma_{n_2,n_1}(A)= \sup_{ k\geq n_2}\frac{\log\left(N_{\delta_k}\left(\spec(A)\right)\right)}{\log(1/\delta_k)}.
$$

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Keep the inner limit expressed using the cover counts, then use the logarithmic factor-three bound to prove directly that its outer limit equals the required limsup or liminf.
issues.overall_effect: The stated box-dimension classifications are not established by the displayed inference as written, and the S2 lower-box classification later invokes this proof.
issues.title: Box-counting proof identifies cover counts with spectrum counts
issues.why_classification: The existing comparison estimate supplies a short local correction and preserves all claimed classifications.

diagnostic_evidence.quote:
\mathrm{dist}(z,\spec(A))\leq \Phi_n(z,A),\quad \lim_{n\rightarrow \infty}\Phi_n(z,A)=\mathrm{dist}(z,\spec(A)),
$$
where the convergence is uniform on compact subsets of $\mathbb{R}$.
For any fixed $n_2$, $z$ and $A$, $\widehat{\Phi}_{n_1}(n_2;z,A)$ is eventually constant for large $n_1$.

issues.failure_explanation: The radii are rounded versions of upper bounds on the true distance, so at finite $n_1$ they can exceed $\dist(w,\spec(A))$ and their open balls can contain spectral points. Local uniform convergence does not control newly introduced grid points with $|w|$ growing with $n_1$, and pointwise eventual constancy at each fixed $w$ does not imply eventual constancy of the whole expanding union. For example, with spectrum $\{0\}$, S2 permits computable functions equal to $|z|$ on every eventually fixed compact set but arbitrarily large for $|z|$ comparable to $n$; a ball centered near $n$ can then cover all of $[-n,n]$ for every $n$. Thus the constructed sets may remain empty and need not cover the spectrum.

failure_location.quote:
For any fixed $n_2$ and $A$, $\Gamma_{n_2,n_1}^\spec(A)$ is eventually constant for large $n_1$ and the limit set $\Gamma_{n_2}^\spec(A)=\lim_{n_1\rightarrow\infty}\Gamma_{n_2,n_1}^\spec(A)$ satisfies
$
\spec(A)\subset \Gamma_{n_2}^\spec(A) \subset \spec(A)+B_{2/n_2}(0),
$

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, a repair must construct genuine spectral covers from the one-sided distance approximants while controlling the expanding spatial grid and must re-establish the stated limit counts.
issues.overall_effect: The claimed conversion from S2 to S1 fails, so all S2 classifications obtained by passing this construction into the S1 results are unsupported.
issues.title: The S2 hole-drilling construction can remove the spectrum
issues.why_classification: The covering lemma is the global bridge underlying the entire S2 theory, and the available assumptions do not support its construction. Repair requires a substantially new construction or stronger assumptions.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: For any fixed $n_2$, $z$ and $A$, $\widehat{\Phi}_{n_1}(n_2;z,A)$ is eventually constant for large $n_1$.

issues.failure_explanation: Even if the covering lemma were repaired for each fixed resolution, its argument supplies only stabilization with the resolution fixed. It does not give a stabilization index uniform in $n$, as asserted here. The maximum simultaneously introduces finer resolutions $k$ as $n_1$ grows, so pointwise convergence in each fixed $k$ cannot be interchanged with this expanding maximum without a uniform convergence or diagonal estimate.

failure_location.quote:
\cref{lem:cover1}'s proof shows there exists $M\in\mathbb{N}$ with $\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,m}(A)\subset\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,m+1}(A)$ for all $m\geq M$, independent of $n$. Hence,
$$
\lim_{n_1\rightarrow\infty}\max_{n_2\leq k\leq n_1} \frac{\log(N_{2^{-k}}(\widetilde{\Gamma}_{k+1,n_1}(A)))}{\log(2^k)}=\sup_{k\geq n_2} \frac{\log(N_{2^{-k}}(\widetilde{\Gamma}_{k+1}(A)))}{\log(2^k)}.
$$

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, prove convergence uniform over all resolutions entering the expanding maximum, or introduce an additional limit to separate cover stabilization from the box-counting limsup.
issues.overall_effect: The claimed $\Pi_2^A$ classifications for the upper box-counting dimension and, on $\widehat\Omega$, the box-counting dimension remain unsupported independently of the basic covering-lemma defect.
issues.title: The diagonal limit used for the upper box dimension lacks uniform control
issues.why_classification: The evident fallback adds a limit and materially worsens the highlighted SCI classification; the source provides no argument preserving the advertised lower complexity.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: We can use the functions $\Phi_n$ constructed in \cref{sec:bounded_disp} to measure the error of the finite section and tiling methods. \cref{fig:Pen_FS_error} shows the maximum error for different truncation sizes of the tile, where we have computed the error using $\Phi_{10^6}$, corresponding to a truncation size of $10^6$.

For each model, we see heavy spectral pollution of the finite section and tiling methods: areas where the “convergent algorithm” signals no spectrum, but the “finite tiling” or “finite section” methods produce spectrum.

issues.failure_explanation: The computed $\Phi_{10^6}$ is an upper bound on distance to the spectrum, not a lower bound. A large or stagnant value therefore does not certify that an alleged finite-section eigenvalue stays away from the true spectrum, and finite discrepancies cannot prove asymptotic nonconvergence. Likewise, absence from a finite output of a convergent approximation does not by itself certify absence from the spectrum.

failure_location.quote: We see that neither the finite section nor the tiling methods converge.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Recast the observations as finite-resolution numerical discrepancies, or provide certified lower bounds on distance from the relevant finite-section eigenvalues to the spectrum and a separate asymptotic argument proving nonconvergence.
issues.overall_effect: The numerical section's assertions of demonstrated spectral pollution and failure of convergence are stronger than what the stated one-sided estimates establish.
issues.title: Finite upper-distance computations do not prove spectral pollution or nonconvergence
issues.why_classification: The algorithms and formal SCI results need not be abandoned, but the advertised interpretation of the numerical experiment must be materially weakened unless new certification and asymptotic analysis are supplied.
